name: PhonePe
summary: Candidates commonly report that PhonePe's engineering interviews include problem-solving rounds, a machine coding or low-level design round and, for experienced roles, system design, often around payments at very large scale: reliability, latency and correctness. PhonePe publishes 14 value statements on its careers site, starting with integrity and honesty, and covering ownership, first-principles thinking and customers as its primary stakeholders.
rounds: Online coding test or recruiter screen
Problem-solving / data structures interviews, often two
Machine coding or low-level design round (for many engineering roles)
Hiring manager round, often on ownership and past work
looks_for: Integrity and honesty, which PhonePe calls the price of admission
Customers as the first and primary stakeholders
Owning problems fully, even across team boundaries
Understanding the whole problem and building from first principles
Removing complexity instead of living with it
Quality and impact of work over busywork
Open-mindedness, and voicing unpopular views backed by data and logic

questions.text: Tell me about a time you fixed a problem that wasn't strictly your team's job.
covers: The problem, and why no one owned it
What you did, including working with the team that did own that area
The result, and how ownership was made clear afterwards

questions.text: Describe a time you removed complexity from a system or process instead of working around it.
covers: What was complex and what it cost: bugs, slow changes, confusion
How you simplified it and got others to agree
What was easier or faster afterwards, with a number if you have one

questions.text: Tell me about a time you held an unpopular view at work. How did you make your case?
covers: The view and why most people disagreed
The data or reasoning you used
What was decided, and whether you were right

questions.text: Tell me about a time doing the right thing made a deadline harder. What did you do?
covers: The shortcut and why it wasn't right
How you explained the cost of doing it properly
The outcome and what others took from it

questions.text: How would you design a UPI payment flow so the user can tell at every moment whether their money has gone?
covers: Clear states (started, pending, succeeded, failed) and what the screen says for each
Callbacks from the bank plus status checks when a reply is late
Timeouts, automatic reversals and a notification when a pending payment settles

questions.text: How would you design a transaction history service for a payments app with a very large number of users?
covers: Writing entries from payment events, stored by user and time
Fast reads: pagination, caching recent items, search and filters
Staying consistent with the payment records, and handling late updates

questions.text: A request has to call five other services before it can reply. What happens to speed and reliability, and how would you design around it?
covers: Slow calls and failures add up across the chain
Timeouts, limited retries and circuit breakers
Calling in parallel, caching, and moving work off the request path where possible

questions.text: How would you design a rate limiter for a busy payments API that runs on many servers?
covers: An algorithm such as token bucket or sliding window, and why
Shared counters in a fast store, and whether approximate counts are acceptable
Limits per user or per merchant, and what the caller sees when limited

questions.text: During a festival, payment success rates dip for a few minutes and then recover. How would you find the cause afterwards?
covers: Building a timeline from metrics, logs and traces
Checking what changed: a deploy, a partner bank, a traffic spike, a database
The root cause and what prevents it next time: capacity, alerts, fallbacks

questions.text: In a machine coding round, how would you model a simple wallet with add money, pay and refund so it's easy to extend?
covers: Classes for wallet, transaction and ledger entries, with the balance derived from entries
Interfaces where new payment methods or rules could plug in
Two payments at once on one wallet, and a few tests that show it works

questions.text: How would you measure whether a new bill-splitting feature is a success?
covers: One main metric, such as how many users split a bill again within a month
Guardrails: failed payments, complaints, effect on other payments
How you'd test it, and what result would make you change course

questions.text: Why PhonePe? Which of its values matters most to you, and when have you lived it?
covers: A reason tied to the product or its users, not only the brand
One value in your own words, with a short example
Why that way of working suits you

questions.text: Which PhonePe feature would you improve, and how would you know it helped users?
covers: A specific feature and a real user problem with it
The change and what you'd leave out
The metric that would show it worked

tips: PhonePe's values call integrity the price of admission; describe your real part in each story, including mistakes.
Prepare to talk about scale and failure: timeouts, retries, slow partner banks, and what users see while a payment is pending.
For machine coding, practise building a small, extensible system (a wallet, a rate limiter, a cache) in a set time, with clean classes and a quick demo.
Building from first principles is one of its stated values; restate the problem and its limits in your own words before you design.

sources.title: Life at PhonePe: Our Values (PhonePe Careers)
